data.name: Dishonored 2
data.detailed_description:
Free Bonus Content



Logging in with your account will get you the following new modes in Dishonored 2:

Mission+
Take a trip back in time to any previously completed mission from the campaign and experiment freely with all powers and weapons.

Black and White
Feeling moody? Black and White mode lets you experience the game in a new visual style. This filter does exactly what it says on the tin, but all blood will remain red. See? Moody. You can toggle between Black and White mode and the original color mode at any time.

In addition to these two new modes, Dishonored 2 players who log in with their account will also gain access to the original pre-order bonus, the Imperial Assassin’s Pack. When you stop by the Dreadful Wale, you’ll find all the bonus items in the pack waiting for you in your cabin.

The Imperial Assassin’s Pack includes:

  • Duelist’s Luck bone charm
  • Void Favor bone charm
  • In-game Antique Serkonan Guitar for Emily or Corvo to interact with
  • In-game book: Goodbye, Karnaca – A Musician’s Farewell
  • 500 bonus coins


This Year's Breakout Game

Winner, Best Action Adventure Game, The Game Awards 2016


Acerca do jogo

Game Description

Reprise your role as a supernatural assassin in Dishonored 2.

Praised by PC Gamer as “brilliant”, IGN as “amazing” and “a superb sequel”, declared a “masterpiece” by Eurogamer, and hailed “a must-play revenge tale among the best in its class” by Game Informer, Dishonored 2 is the follow up to Arkane Studio's first-person action blockbuster and winner of more than 100 'Game of the Year' awards, Dishonored.

Play your way in a world where mysticism and industry collide. Will you choose to play as Empress Emily Kaldwin or the royal protector, Corvo Attano? Will you make your way through the game unseen, make full use of its brutal combat system, or use a blend of both? How will you combine your character's unique set of powers, weapons and gadgets to eliminate your enemies? The story responds to your choices, leading to intriguing outcomes, as you play through each of the game's hand-crafted missions.

Story

Dishonored 2 is set 15 years after the Lord Regent has been vanquished and the dreaded Rat Plague has passed into history. An otherworldly usurper has seized Empress Emily Kaldwin’s throne, leaving the fate of the Isles hanging in the balance. As Emily or Corvo, travel beyond the legendary streets of Dunwall to Karnaca, the once-dazzling coastal city that holds the keys to restoring Emily to power. Armed with the Mark of the Outsider and powerful new abilities, track down your enemies and take back what’s rightfully yours.

Key Features

  • The Assassins

    As fully voiced characters, Emily Kaldwin and Corvo Attano now bring their own perspectives and emotional responses to the world and story. Use each character’s set of powers, gadgets and uniquely-tuned weapons in creative ways as you explore the world – whether you fight your way through the city streets or sneak across the rooftops - and which enemies you decide to eliminate or spare.

  • Supernatural Powers

    Advanced bonecharm crafting and all-new upgrade trees allow you to customize your powers in vastly different ways. Become a living shadow to silently stalk your targets, link enemies so they share a common fate, or mesmerize your foes and dominate their minds. Choose from nearly infinite combinations of violence, nonlethal combat, powers and weapons to accomplish your objectives.

  • Imaginative World

    From the grimy, rat-infested streets of Dunwall to the lush, exotic coasts of a decaying Karnaca, immerse yourself in stylized locales created by Arkane’s premiere art and narrative teams. The world is a character in its own right, rich with story, architecture and eclectic characters. It is also punctuated by signature mission locations, such as the Dust District, ravaged by dust storms and warring factions, and a madman’s mansion made of shifting walls, deadly traps and clockwork soldiers.

  • The Void Engine

    Dishonored 2 is beautifully brought to life with the new Void Engine, a leap forward in rendering technology, built from id Tech and highly-customized by Arkane Studios. Designed to support world-class art direction and take full advantage of the powerful hardware this generation has to offer, the Void Engine allows for significant advances to all game systems, including responsive stealth and combat Artificial Intelligence, lighting and graphical rendering, impressively dense urban environments, and story presentation.

reviews.review:
[h1]Play Your Way[/h1] 
There's something wrong with these Dishonored games that bothers me endlessly while playing. It's a game design pillar that on its face seems enticing and agreeable, but in practice clashes hard with my enjoyment of the game. It's this notion of "play your way" which is in reference to the dichotomy of action and stealth or high chaos and low chaos. Players are free to tackle problems their way: do you go in guns-a-blazing or ghost the level not having a soul lay eyes on you?

So here's the predicament I find myself, and this is speaking from how I interpret and interface with a game like this, the high chaos, action version of Dishonored 2 is incredibly fun mechanically but morally wrong while the stealthy, low chaos version gets you a better ending but turns the game into trial and error. Disclaimer: I really do not like using quick save/load, it destroys immersion and any gameplay rhythm you've established. So, on a first playthrough, and I don't care how good you are, you are going to be seen by the enemy and they are going to aggressively hunt your ass. It is at this point that the high chaos demon appears on my one shoulder and the low chaos angel appears on the other. The high chaos demon tells me to rip and tear, jump off the ledge, smack their skull into the pavement, whip out the pistol, shoot the next guard's knee out, jump and stab my sword into their chest, use 'Far Reach' to pull the officer off the balcony and slice him midair… You get the point: use your substantial arsenal of weapons and powers to lay waste to those who stand between you and your objective. Meanwhile the low chaos angel on the other shoulder tells me to run and hide, maybe if there's only one or two guards, slip out of sight then pounce when they've turned around and incapacitate them.

So why not just go for the action-heavy, mechanically fun route and kill anyone that lays eyes on you? Well, you play as an empress who's been overthrown and now wanted. In the first level, which is essentially the coup and immediate fallout, I had no problem hunting down and slaughtering my betrayers, it felt justified. But then you travel to another city and begin sneaking through alleyways and apartments and you overhear conversations and little interactions that bring humanity to the common folk. I appreciate these off the cuff moments you can observe and overhear and as the empress of these people you feel a responsibility to them and she'll even comment on this sometimes. Moral of the story is my zeal for revenge wore off completely and fairly quickly making the high chaos path seem completely psychotic. What decent empress would ever go full-Doom Slayer mode and glory kill the guard who's just doing his job standing at a checkpoint, remarking about how he misses his kids and hopes to see them soon? Maybe some people find this compelling, I find it confusing. I feel like there had to be an alternate way to frame the main character, story, or high chaos route to make it be less psychotic of a path.

I ended up falling somewhere in between the two extremes. I wasn't good enough or knowledgeable enough yet to ghost the levels and the murderous route didn't feel right. So, I ended up choking out a lot of guards, getting caught and running away, and using traps and contraptions to confuse and get around certain bottlenecks. But every now and then I had to feed that base urge to slaughter my enemy. Probably about once a level, upon being caught, instead of running away or trying to silently deal with the guard I would simply stand up, draw out my sword and pistol and stand and fight. A bloodbath would ensue, severed limbs, decapitations, shattered bone, ripping souls from flesh… And then I'd pause and reload from the last auto-save, that wasn't the real empress, that was the high chaos demon on her shoulder taking too much control.

So, how would I attempt to fix this problem? I would go after high/low chaos being too binary while also being too vague. Here are two actions: bombing guards and civilians in the street with a whale oil tank versus silently assassinating witches and nest keepers in a secluded mansion. The issue here is that from a chaos perspective, I have no idea which is higher chaos, but from a morality standpoint the answer is abundantly clear. Here's another one: is stopping the pair of civilians about to bomb the foundation of a high-rise to get into a black market the same as murdering a homeless guy in the street? I don't know! To summarize my point here, this "morality" system exists and has consequences, that's cool, so make it make sense for who you're playing as: an empress on the run. I think detections and who you're killing should matter in the chaos system. Shouldn't getting the evil, destructive witches out of here help the common folk? Isn't that what the chaos system is about? Better outcomes for the commoners?

[h1] "That level design... oh that level design"[/h1] 
Other than this tiny quibble over the "play your way" game design, I found Dishonored 2 to be a rather exceptional game. Where to start? Well, the level design is the star of the show, and my god is it glorious. It's just a handful of levels but each are exceptional in their own right, memorable and distinct from the rest. First I'll point out, and this goes for all the levels, the world of Dishonored feels lived in and immersive. Civilians roam the streets going about their business, out on the docks bitching to one another, having hushed conversations in an alleyway. You can happen upon little scenes that unfold seemingly naturally but are surely planned out so that an attentive player overhears them. In the Overseer's headquarters you can observe one overseer mercifully ending their friend's life as they were succumbing to previous injuries. In the first level you can find a guard trying to pressure the editor of the local newspaper into publishing a particular headline. In the area leading up to Jindosh's mansion you can come across a couple of ladies talking about robbing some place. Later you can find them stacking explosives behind the black market shop. And this leads into the part of the "play your way" Immersive Sim design philosophy that I enjoy much more: problem-solving the level. I mean this on both a macro and micro scale. I like the classic Prey test: can you get past this locked door? I also like the classic Dishonored test: how will you get around this guard checkpoint in the town square? The high chaos, low chaos question is still there, but there's also a lot of level design pieces and little gameplay mechanics that work their way into that as well. Do you find the power source to the wall of light and rip it out? Do you find and work your way through a quarantined apartment complex that's infested with bloodflies? Do you find a secret rat passage in the alleyway that you can move through in your phantom form? Do you steal a guard's key ring so that you can unlock and sneak into their guardhouse? Do you rewire the light wall or guard tower to set the equipment against the guards? Choices and creativity abound and I love it.

When Arkane were designing the scope of the game, the story, the gameplay, etc. it feels like a lot of love and focus was poured into these levels. There's nine in total and outside of the first, intro level in Dunwall, simply put, they're all bangers. There's barely a dip in quality anywhere. What an accomplishment.

Read the full review [url=https://www.sevastromo.com/dishonored-2/] HERE [/url]
